connection: Session 10 established the prerequisite model. This session applies it to keyed collections with observable TimeLedger examples.
objectives: Explain dictionaries map unique keys to values while hash sets represent unique membership.
Predict behavior before running a focused keyed collections example.
Apply dictionaries, sets, and lookup semantics without weakening existing domain invariants.
Verify the behavior with automated tests.

concept.title: Build the behavioral model
paragraphs: The central rule is that dictionaries map unique keys to values while hash sets represent unique membership.
Names and syntax matter because they communicate whether code copies, aliases, enumerates, compares, or constrains a value.
concept.code:
Dictionary<string, Worker> workers = new();
HashSet<string> teams = new();

concept.title: Program to the required capability
paragraphs: A caller should not need to provide more capability than the operation consumes.
Concrete implementations remain useful at construction boundaries; interfaces and generic contracts keep consuming code focused.
concept.code:
// Prefer the smallest contract that supports the operation.
Dictionary<string, Worker> workers = new();

concept.title: Verify cause and effect
paragraphs: The lab changes one behavior at a time and uses tests to preserve the observation.
If the prediction differs from the result, explain the language rule before continuing.

lab.objective: Add a focused TimeLedger example that demonstrates dictionaries, sets, and lookup semantics.
lab.startingCondition: Sessions 01–10 are complete and the solution builds with all existing tests passing.
steps: Read the starting test and predict the result using the session mental model.
Add src/TimeLedger.Domain/WorkerDirectory.cs with the smallest API needed for the example.
Add tests/TimeLedger.Domain.Tests/WorkerDirectoryTests.cs to check the important before-and-after behavior.
Run the focused tests, then run the complete Release test suite.
Review whether each parameter and return type exposes only the capability it needs.
lab.expectedBehavior: The new tests demonstrate dictionaries map unique keys to values while hash sets represent unique membership; all existing behavior remains green.
lab.validation: dotnet build TimeLedger.sln --configuration Release && dotnet test TimeLedger.sln --configuration Release

Which compiler error or test most clearly reveals the contract?

whatBreaks: Removing the new domain example removes the executable model for keyed collections. Removing its tests allows subtle changes to assignment, equality, enumeration, or generic contracts to pass unnoticed. Widening the API unnecessarily gives callers capabilities the operation does not need.
summary: This session established that dictionaries map unique keys to values while hash sets represent unique membership. The TimeLedger example, tests, and API review turn that rule into durable engineering practice.
